CT ‖ a_{k} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) e^{−jkω_{o.title: Fourier series analysis (continuous time)
CT ‖ a_{k} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) e^{−jkω_{o.about: Finds how much of each harmonic e^{jkω_{o}t} a periodic signal contains. Integrate over any one period; a_{0} is the signal's average value.
assumptions: x(t) is periodic with period T
Dirichlet conditions: x is absolutely integrable over a period, with finitely many extrema and discontinuities per period
At a jump the series converges to the midpoint
vars: complex amplitude of the k-th harmonic
related: synthesis: rebuild x from its coefficients

example.problem: Find a_{k} for x(t) = cos(ω_{o}t) + 2 sin(3ω_{o}t).
steps: Write each term with Euler: cos(ω_{o}t) = (1/2)e^{jω_{o}t} + (1/2)e^{−jω_{o}t}
Read off the coefficients (the integral gives the same): a_{±1} = 1/2, a_{3} = 1/j = −j, a_{−3} = j

DT ‖ a_{k} = (1/N) Σ_{n=<N>} x[n] e^{−jk.title: Fourier series analysis (discrete time)
DT ‖ a_{k} = (1/N) Σ_{n=<N>} x[n] e^{−jk.about: Finds the N coefficients of a periodic sequence by summing over any one period. Unlike the CT series there are only N distinct coefficients, and a_{k} repeats every N.
assumptions: x[n] is periodic with period N
The sum runs over any N consecutive n

example.problem: x[n] has period 4 with one period {1, 1, 0, 0} for n = 0..3. Find a_{1}.

CT ‖ x(t) = Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o.title: Fourier series synthesis (continuous time)
CT ‖ x(t) = Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o.about: Rebuilds a periodic signal as a sum of harmonics at multiples of the fundamental frequency, each weighted by its coefficient a_{k}.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with period T and satisfying the Dirichlet conditions
The infinite sum converges to x(t) where x is continuous and to the midpoint at a jump
For real x, a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*} and the pair of terms ±k add to a real cosine

example.problem: A signal of period T = 2π has a_{0} = 1, a_{±1} = 1/2 and no other coefficients. What is x(0) and x(π)?

DT ‖ x[n] = Σ_{k=<N>} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o}n}.title: Fourier series synthesis (discrete time)
DT ‖ x[n] = Σ_{k=<N>} a_{k} e^{jkω_{o}n}.about: Rebuilds a periodic sequence from its N coefficients. The sum is finite, so it is exact, with no convergence question.
assumptions: Sum over any N consecutive values of k

x(t) = A_{0} + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} [A_{k} cos(kω.title: Trigonometric Fourier series
x(t) = A_{0} + Σ_{k=1}^{∞} [A_{k} cos(kω.about: The real-valued form of the Fourier series: a periodic real signal as its average plus cosines and sines at multiples of the fundamental.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic with period T
Even signals have only cosines (B_{k} = 0); odd signals only sines (A_{0} = A_{k} = 0)

example.problem: A square wave of period T, +1 for the first half and −1 for the second (odd), has B_{k} = 4/(πk) for odd k and nothing else. Find the amplitude of its first three nonzero harmonics.
steps: A_{0} = 0 and A_{k} = 0 because the wave is odd with zero average

A_{0} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) dt.title: DC term of the trig Fourier series
A_{0} = (1/T) ∫_{T} x(t) dt.about: The constant term is the signal's average over one period. It equals a_{0} in the exponential form.
assumptions: Integrate over any one full period
related: same number in the exponential form

example.problem: A pulse train is 5 V for 2 ms out of every 8 ms period and 0 V otherwise. Find A_{0}.
steps: A_{0} = (1/8 ms) ∫ over the period = (5 V × 2 ms)/(8 ms)

A_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) cos(kω_{o}t) dt.title: Cosine coefficients of the trig Fourier series
A_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) cos(kω_{o}t) dt.about: Projects the signal onto cos(kω_{o}t) to find the amplitude of the k-th cosine harmonic. The factor is 2/T, not 1/T, because a cosine's mean square is 1/2.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic with period T

example.problem: Find A_{1} for the even pulse train x(t) = 1 for |t| < T/4, 0 elsewhere in the period.

B_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) sin(kω_{o}t) dt.title: Sine coefficients of the trig Fourier series
B_{k} = (2/T) ∫_{T} x(t) sin(kω_{o}t) dt.about: Projects the signal onto sin(kω_{o}t) to find the amplitude of the k-th sine harmonic.
assumptions: x(t) real and periodic with period T

example.problem: Find B_{k} for the square wave that is +1 on (0, T/2) and −1 on (T/2, T).
steps: = 4/(kπ) for odd k, 0 for even k; B_{3} = 4/(3π) ≈ 0.424

a_{k} = (A_{k} − jB_{k})/2.title: Exponential coefficients from trig coefficients
a_{k} = (A_{k} − jB_{k})/2.about: Converts the real cosine and sine amplitudes of harmonic k into the complex exponential coefficient. The magnitude |a_{k}| is half the harmonic's amplitude.
related: A_{k} = 2 Re a_{k}, B_{k} = −2 Im a_{k}

example.problem: Harmonic 2 of a real signal is 3 cos(2ω_{o}t) + 4 sin(2ω_{o}t). Find a_{2} and its magnitude.

a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}.title: Conjugate symmetry of Fourier coefficients
a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}.about: For a real signal the coefficient at −k is the complex conjugate of the one at +k, so |a_{k}| is even in k and ∠a_{k} is odd. You only need k ≥ 0.
assumptions: If x is also even, a_{k} is real and even; if odd, a_{k} is imaginary and odd
related: the same symmetry for the Fourier transform

example.problem: A real signal has a_{3} = 2 − j. Find a_{−3}, and check the pair adds to a real signal.

x(t − t_{0}) ‖ a_{k} e^{−jkω_{o}t_{0}}.title: Time shift (Fourier series property)
x(t − t_{0}) ‖ a_{k} e^{−jkω_{o}t_{0}}.about: Delaying a periodic signal by t_{0} leaves each coefficient's magnitude alone and adds a phase of −kω_{o}t_{0}, linear in k.
assumptions: x(t) periodic with period T and coefficients a_{k}

example.problem: x(t) has period T = 1 s and a_{1} = 1. Find the new a_{1} after delaying x by 0.25 s.

x(−t) ‖ a_{−k}.title: Time reversal (Fourier series property)
x(−t) ‖ a_{−k}.about: Flipping a periodic signal in time swaps its coefficients at k and −k.
assumptions: For real x, a_{−k} = a_{k}^{*}, so reversal conjugates the coefficients
An even x has a_{−k} = a_{k}; an odd x has a_{−k} = −a_{k}

example.problem: x(t) has a_{1} = 2j and a_{−1} = −2j (that is, x = −4 sin(ω_{o}t)). Find the coefficients of x(−t).
steps: So x(−t) = 4 sin(ω_{o}t), as sin is odd

dx/dt ‖ jkω_{o} a_{k}.title: Differentiation (Fourier series property)
dx/dt ‖ jkω_{o} a_{k}.about: Differentiating a periodic signal multiplies harmonic k by jkω_{o}: higher harmonics grow and the DC term disappears.
assumptions: x(t) periodic and differentiable (impulses allowed at jumps)

example.problem: x(t) = 3 cos(100t), so a_{±1} = 1.5 with ω_{o} = 100 rad/s. Find the coefficient of dx/dt at k = 1.

x(t) y(t) ‖ Σ_{l} a_{l} b_{k−l}.title: Multiplication (Fourier series property)
x(t) y(t) ‖ Σ_{l} a_{l} b_{k−l}.about: The product of two signals with the same period has coefficients equal to the discrete convolution of their coefficient sequences.
assumptions: x and y periodic with the same period T
a_{k} are x's coefficients and b_{k} are y's

example.problem: x = cos(ω_{o}t) has a_{±1} = 1/2. Find the coefficients of x^{2}.

(1/T) ∫_{T} |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ Σ_{k} |a_{k}.title: Parseval's relation for Fourier series
(1/T) ∫_{T} |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ Σ_{k} |a_{k}.about: The average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of the squared magnitudes of its coefficients, so each harmonic contributes |a_{k}|^{2} to the power.

example.problem: x(t) = 2 + 3 cos(ω_{o}t). Find its average power.

e^{jθ} = cos(θ) + j sin(θ).title: Euler's formula
e^{jθ} = cos(θ) + j sin(θ).about: Links the complex exponential to cosine and sine: e^{jθ} is the point at angle θ on the unit circle. Every polar-form and phasor calculation rests on it.
assumptions: θ real (it also holds for complex θ)

example.problem: Write e^{j2π/3} in rectangular form.

e^{jθ} + e^{−jθ} = 2 cos(θ).title: Sum of conjugate exponentials
e^{jθ} + e^{−jθ} = 2 cos(θ).about: Adding e^{jθ} and its conjugate cancels the imaginary parts and leaves twice the cosine. This is why a real cosine has two spectral lines at ±ω.

example.problem: Evaluate e^{jπ/3} + e^{−jπ/3}.

e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ} = 2j sin(θ).title: Difference of conjugate exponentials
e^{jθ} − e^{−jθ} = 2j sin(θ).about: Subtracting cancels the real parts and leaves 2j times the sine.

example.problem: Evaluate e^{jπ/6} − e^{−jπ/6}.

cos(θ) = (1/2) e^{jθ} + (1/2) e^{−jθ}.title: Cosine as complex exponentials
cos(θ) = (1/2) e^{jθ} + (1/2) e^{−jθ}.about: Splits a cosine into two counter-rotating phasors of half amplitude. Use it to find Fourier coefficients or transforms of sinusoids by inspection.
assumptions: θ real (holds for complex θ too)

example.problem: Find the Fourier series coefficients of 6 cos(4t + π/3).

sin(θ) = (1/2j) e^{jθ} − (1/2j) e^{−jθ}.title: Sine as complex exponentials
sin(θ) = (1/2j) e^{jθ} − (1/2j) e^{−jθ}.about: Splits a sine into two phasors with coefficients ±1/(2j) = ∓j/2.
assumptions: θ real (holds for complex θ too)

example.problem: Find the Fourier series coefficients of 4 sin(10t).

(cos θ + j sin θ)^{n} = cos(nθ) + j sin(.title: De Moivre's theorem
(cos θ + j sin θ)^{n} = cos(nθ) + j sin(.about: Raising a unit complex number to a power multiplies its angle by the power. It follows from (e^{jθ})^{n} = e^{jnθ}.
assumptions: n an integer (for non-integer n the power has several values)

example.problem: Find (cos 30° + j sin 30°)^{6}.

cos^{2}(A) = 1/2 + (1/2) cos(2A).title: Cosine squared (power reduction)
cos^{2}(A) = 1/2 + (1/2) cos(2A).about: Turns a squared cosine into a constant plus a cosine at twice the frequency. Useful for average power and for squaring a sinusoid.

example.problem: Find cos^{2}(π/8).

sin^{2}(A) = 1/2 − (1/2) cos(2A).title: Sine squared (power reduction)
sin^{2}(A) = 1/2 − (1/2) cos(2A).about: Turns a squared sine into a constant minus a cosine at twice the frequency; its average over a period is 1/2.

example.problem: Find the average of sin^{2}(ωt) and sin^{2}(π/12).
steps: The cos(2ωt) term averages to 0, so the mean is 1/2

cos(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) + cos(A.title: Product of cosines
cos(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) + cos(A.about: Multiplying two sinusoids gives the difference and sum frequencies. This is the heart of mixing and AM modulation.

example.problem: A 1000 Hz tone is multiplied by a 100 kHz carrier. What frequencies come out, and what is cos(1)cos(2)?

sin(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) − cos(A.title: Product of sines
sin(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[cos(A − B) − cos(A.about: Turns a product of sines into a difference of cosines at the difference and sum angles.

example.problem: Find sin(1) sin(2) with the identity.

sin(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A.title: Product of sine and cosine
sin(A) cos(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A.about: Turns sine times cosine into a sum of sines at the sum and difference angles.

example.problem: Find sin(2) cos(1) with the identity.

cos(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) − sin(A.title: Product of cosine and sine
cos(A) sin(B) = (1/2)[sin(A + B) − sin(A.about: Turns cosine times sine into a difference of sines at the sum and difference angles.

example.problem: Find cos(2) sin(1) with the identity.

e^{j0} = 1.title: Zero angle on the unit circle
e^{j0} = 1.about: A phasor with zero angle is the real number 1: no rotation, unit length.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: A phasor is 5e^{j0}. Write it in rectangular form.

e^{±j2π} = 1.title: A full turn on the unit circle
e^{±j2π} = 1.about: Rotating by a full turn in either direction brings you back to 1. This is why complex exponentials are periodic in angle with period 2π.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Simplify e^{j(π/3 + 2π)}.

e^{±jπ} = −1.title: Half a turn on the unit circle
e^{±jπ} = −1.about: A rotation of π either way lands on −1; e^{jπ} + 1 = 0 is Euler's identity. Multiplying by −1 is a 180° phase shift.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: A signal 4e^{j(ωt + π)} is how many times 4e^{jωt}?

e^{jπ/2} = j.title: Quarter turn counter-clockwise
e^{jπ/2} = j.about: Multiplying by j rotates a phasor 90° counter-clockwise. That is why an inductor's impedance jωL leads by 90°.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Rotate 3 + 4j by +90°.

e^{−jπ/2} = −j.title: Quarter turn clockwise
e^{−jπ/2} = −j.about: Multiplying by −j rotates a phasor 90° clockwise. A capacitor's impedance 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC) lags by 90°.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Rotate 3 + 4j by −90°.

e^{jπ/4} = (1 + j)/√2.title: 45° on the unit circle
e^{jπ/4} = (1 + j)/√2.about: At 45° the real and imaginary parts are equal, each 1/√2 ≈ 0.7071.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Write 10e^{jπ/4} in rectangular form.

e^{jπ/3} = (1 + j√3)/2.title: 60° on the unit circle
e^{jπ/3} = (1 + j√3)/2.about: At 60° the real part is 1/2 and the imaginary part √3/2 ≈ 0.866.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Write 2e^{jπ/3} in rectangular form.

e^{jπ/6} = (√3 + j)/2.title: 30° on the unit circle
e^{jπ/6} = (√3 + j)/2.about: At 30° the real part is √3/2 ≈ 0.866 and the imaginary part 1/2.
assumptions: Every e^{jθ} lies on the unit circle, |e^{jθ}| = 1

example.problem: Write 4e^{jπ/6} in rectangular form.

e^{j0t} = 1.title: A zero-frequency exponential is constant
e^{j0t} = 1.about: A complex exponential at ω = 0 does not rotate; it is the constant 1 for all t. This is the DC term (k = 0) of a Fourier series.

example.problem: What is the k = 0 term of a Fourier series with a_{0} = 3?

e^{jπk} = e^{−jπk} = (−1)^{k}.title: Integer multiples of π
e^{jπk} = e^{−jπk} = (−1)^{k}.about: An integer number of half-turns alternates between +1 and −1. It shows up all over Fourier series and DT signals, for example e^{jπn} = (−1)^{n} is the fastest DT oscillation.

example.problem: Simplify e^{j3π} and e^{−j4π}.

e^{±j2πk} = 1.title: Integer multiples of a full turn
e^{±j2πk} = 1.about: Any whole number of full turns returns to 1. This makes DT frequencies repeat every 2π and DFT bins repeat every N.
related: DT frequencies are periodic, n an integer

example.problem: Show that e^{j(0.5 + 2π)n} = e^{j0.5n} for integer n, using n = 3.

j^{2} = −1.title: The imaginary unit squared
j^{2} = −1.about: The defining property of j (engineers use j because i is current). Use it to simplify every product of complex numbers.

example.problem: Multiply (2 + 3j)(4 − j).

1/j = −j.title: Reciprocal of j
1/j = −j.about: Dividing by j is the same as multiplying by −j, a 90° clockwise rotation. Handy for capacitor impedance and sine coefficients.
assumptions: Multiply top and bottom by j: 1/j = j/j^{2} = −j

example.problem: Find the impedance of a 10 µF capacitor at ω = 1000 rad/s.

j = i.title: j and i are the same imaginary unit
j = i.about: Engineers write j for √(−1) because i means current; mathematicians write i. Q Calc accepts either.

example.problem: Add 3 + 2i and 1 − 5j.
steps: Both units are the same, so add parts: (3 + 1) + (2 − 5)j

z = x + jy = r e^{jθ}.title: Rectangular and polar forms of a complex number
z = x + jy = r e^{jθ}.about: The same complex number written as real and imaginary parts, or as a magnitude and angle. Add in rectangular form; multiply and divide in polar.
assumptions: θ is defined up to multiples of 2π
related: x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ)

example.problem: Write z = −1 + j in polar form.

r = |z| = √(x^{2} + y^{2}).title: Magnitude of a complex number
r = |z| = √(x^{2} + y^{2}).about: The length of z from the origin, by Pythagoras. For a phasor it is the amplitude; for a transfer function it is the gain.

example.problem: Find |3 − 4j|.

θ = atan2(y, x).title: Angle of a complex number
θ = atan2(y, x).about: The angle of z measured counter-clockwise from the positive real axis. atan2 uses the signs of both parts to pick the right quadrant, which atan(y/x) alone cannot.

example.problem: Find the angle of z = −3 − 3j.
steps: Third quadrant: atan(y/x) would wrongly give 45°

x = r cos(θ).title: Real part from polar form
x = r cos(θ).about: Projects a phasor onto the real axis. For a phasor A∠φ, this is the value of A cos(ωt + φ) at t = 0.
assumptions: θ in radians or degrees, consistently

example.problem: Find the real part of 10∠53.13°.

y = r sin(θ).title: Imaginary part from polar form
y = r sin(θ).about: Projects a phasor onto the imaginary axis.
assumptions: θ in radians or degrees, consistently

example.problem: Find the imaginary part of 10∠53.13°.

z_{1} z_{2} = r_{1} r_{2} e^{j(θ_{1} + θ.title: Multiplying in polar form
z_{1} z_{2} = r_{1} r_{2} e^{j(θ_{1} + θ.about: Magnitudes multiply and angles add. Cascading gains in a system works the same way.

example.problem: Multiply 2e^{jπ/6} by 3e^{jπ/3}.

z_{1} / z_{2} = (r_{1}/r_{2}) e^{j(θ_{1}.title: Dividing in polar form
z_{1} / z_{2} = (r_{1}/r_{2}) e^{j(θ_{1}.about: Magnitudes divide and angles subtract. This is how you find a current from a voltage phasor and an impedance.

example.problem: A voltage 10∠30° V drives an impedance 5∠−30° Ω. Find the current.

z^{*} = x − jy = r e^{−jθ}.title: Complex conjugate
z^{*} = x − jy = r e^{−jθ}.about: Flips the sign of the imaginary part, mirroring z across the real axis. The magnitude stays; the angle changes sign.

example.problem: Find the conjugate of 3 + 4j and of 2e^{jπ/5}.

z z^{*} = |z|^{2}.title: A number times its conjugate
z z^{*} = |z|^{2}.about: Gives the squared magnitude, a real number. Used to rationalise a complex denominator and to compute power |X|^{2}.

example.problem: Find 1/(3 + 4j) by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate.

Re z = (z + z^{*})/2.title: Real part from the conjugate
Re z = (z + z^{*})/2.about: Averaging z and its conjugate cancels the imaginary part. This is how a real signal A cos(ωt + φ) is Re{Ae^{jφ}e^{jωt}}.

example.problem: Find Re z for z = 2 − 7j.

Im z = (z − z^{*})/2j.title: Imaginary part from the conjugate
Im z = (z − z^{*})/2j.about: Subtracting the conjugate cancels the real part; dividing by 2j leaves the imaginary part as a real number.

example.problem: Find Im z for z = 2 − 7j.

Analysis ‖ X(jω) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t) e^{−j.title: Continuous-time Fourier transform (analysis)
Analysis ‖ X(jω) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t) e^{−j.about: Breaks an aperiodic signal into a continuum of frequencies. |X(jω)| says how much of frequency ω the signal holds and ∠X(jω) its phase.
assumptions: Exists in the ordinary sense if x is absolutely integrable, ∫|x(t)| dt < ∞
Signals like 1, u(t), cos(ω_{o}t) have transforms only with impulses δ(ω)
related: from the Laplace transform, if the jω axis is in the ROC

example.problem: Find X(jω) for x(t) = e^{−2t}u(t), and its value at ω = 2 rad/s.

Synthesis ‖ x(t) = (1/2π) ∫_{−∞}^{∞} X(j.title: Inverse continuous-time Fourier transform (synthesis)
Synthesis ‖ x(t) = (1/2π) ∫_{−∞}^{∞} X(j.about: Rebuilds the signal from its spectrum as a weighted sum of e^{jωt} over all frequencies. The 1/2π comes from using ω in rad/s.
assumptions: X(jω) is the transform of x(t)
At a jump, the integral returns the midpoint
With f in Hz instead of ω, the 1/2π disappears

example.problem: X(jω) = 1 for |ω| < 10 rad/s and 0 elsewhere. Find x(0).

e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω).title: Decaying exponential and its transform
e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω).about: A one-sided exponential that starts at t = 0 and decays. Its transform is a first-order low-pass: flat below ω = a and falling 20 dB/decade above it. It is the impulse response of an RC circuit.
assumptions: a > 0 (real part positive) so the signal decays; for a ≤ 0 the integral diverges
Holds for complex a with Re a > 0

example.problem: An RC circuit with τ = RC = 1 ms has impulse response (1/τ)e^{−t/τ}u(t). Find |H| at ω = 1000 rad/s.

t e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω)^{2}.title: Ramped exponential and its transform
t e^{−at} u(t), a > 0 ‖ 1/(a + jω)^{2}.about: The exponential multiplied by t: it rises then decays, peaking at t = 1/a. Its transform is a double pole, the response of two identical first-order stages in cascade.

example.problem: Find |X(jω)| for t e^{−3t}u(t) at ω = 4 rad/s.

δ(t) ‖ 1.title: Impulse and its transform
δ(t) ‖ 1.about: A unit impulse contains every frequency equally. That is why a system's impulse response h(t) has transform H(jω), its frequency response.
assumptions: δ(t) is a generalised function with unit area

example.problem: An impulse 3δ(t) enters a system. What is the input's spectrum at ω = 500 rad/s?

δ(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}}.title: Delayed impulse and its transform
δ(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}}.about: A shifted impulse has unit magnitude at all frequencies and a phase falling linearly with ω: a pure delay.

example.problem: Find the transform of δ(t − 2 ms) at ω = 250π rad/s.

1 ‖ 2πδ(ω).title: Constant (DC) signal and its transform
1 ‖ 2πδ(ω).about: A constant has all its energy at ω = 0, so its transform is an impulse there. It is not absolutely integrable, so the transform exists only in the generalised sense.

example.problem: Find the transform of x(t) = 5 V.
steps: An impulse of area 10π ≈ 31.4 at ω = 0

u(t) ‖ 1/(jω) + πδ(ω).title: Unit step and its transform
u(t) ‖ 1/(jω) + πδ(ω).about: The step is the integral of the impulse, so its transform is 1/(jω), plus an impulse for its average value of 1/2.
assumptions: Generalised transform: u(t) is not absolutely integrable
The πδ(ω) term carries the DC value 1/2

example.problem: Find the step's transform at ω = 4 rad/s.

e^{jω_{o}t} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).title: Complex exponential and its transform
e^{jω_{o}t} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).about: A single complex exponential is one spectral line at ω_{o}. Any periodic signal is a sum of these.
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the transform of 3e^{j100t}.
steps: = 6πδ(ω − 100): one line of area 18.85 at ω = 100 rad/s

cos(ω_{o}t) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.title: Cosine and its transform
cos(ω_{o}t) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.about: A cosine is two complex exponentials, so it is two lines of area π at ±ω_{o}.
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the transform of 4 cos(2π·60 t).

sin(ω_{o}t) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.title: Sine and its transform
sin(ω_{o}t) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.about: A sine is two lines at ±ω_{o} with imaginary areas −jπ and +jπ (π/j = −jπ).
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the area of the line at +ω_{o} for 2 sin(ω_{o}t).

sin(Wt)/(πt) ‖ 1 for |ω| < W, 0 else.title: Sinc pulse and the ideal low-pass spectrum
sin(Wt)/(πt) ‖ 1 for |ω| < W, 0 else.about: A sinc in time is a rectangle in frequency. It is the impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter with cutoff W, which is non-causal and so only an ideal.
assumptions: At t = 0 the value is W/π (the limit)

example.problem: An ideal low-pass filter has cutoff W = 2π·1000 rad/s. Find its impulse response's peak h(0).
steps: h(0) = W/π (the area under H divided by 2π)

1 for |t| < T_{1}, 0 else ‖ 2 sin(ωT_{1}.title: Rectangular pulse and its transform
1 for |t| < T_{1}, 0 else ‖ 2 sin(ωT_{1}.about: A pulse of width 2T_{1} has a sinc-shaped spectrum with first zeros at ω = ±π/T_{1}. A shorter pulse spreads wider in frequency.
assumptions: At ω = 0, X = 2T_{1}, the pulse's area

example.problem: A pulse lasts from −1 ms to 1 ms. Find X at ω = 1000 rad/s and the first zero.
steps: First zero at ω = π/T_{1} = 3142 rad/s
example.answer: X(j1000) ≈ 1.683 × 10^{−3} s; first zero at 3142 rad/s

e^{−a|t|}, a > 0 ‖ 2a/(a^{2} + ω^{2}).title: Two-sided exponential and its transform
e^{−a|t|}, a > 0 ‖ 2a/(a^{2} + ω^{2}).about: A symmetric exponential decay has a real, even, Lorentzian spectrum. It is the sum of e^{−at}u(t) and its time reversal.

example.problem: Find X(jω) of e^{−2|t|} at ω = 2 rad/s.

e^{−t^{2}/(2σ^{2})} ‖ σ√(2π) e^{−σ^{2}ω^.title: Gaussian and its transform
e^{−t^{2}/(2σ^{2})} ‖ σ√(2π) e^{−σ^{2}ω^.about: A Gaussian transforms to a Gaussian. Its width in time is σ and in frequency 1/σ, the extreme of the time–bandwidth trade-off.

example.problem: For σ = 0.5 s, find X at ω = 2 rad/s.

Periodic p(t) with F.S. {ω_{o}, a_{k}} ‖.title: Transform of a periodic signal
Periodic p(t) with F.S. {ω_{o}, a_{k}} ‖.about: A periodic signal's transform is a train of impulses at the harmonics kω_{o}, each with area 2π times the Fourier series coefficient.
assumptions: p(t) periodic with a Fourier series

example.problem: A periodic signal has Fourier coefficient a_{1} = −j/π. Find the area of its transform's impulse at ω = ω_{o}.

Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} δ(t − nT) ‖ (2π/T) Σ_{k=−∞}.title: Impulse train and its transform
Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} δ(t − nT) ‖ (2π/T) Σ_{k=−∞}.about: An impulse train with spacing T transforms to an impulse train with spacing 2π/T and area 2π/T. This is the basis of sampling: sampling in time repeats the spectrum every ω_{s} = 2π/T.

example.problem: Sample at 8 kHz. Find the spacing and area of the spectral impulses.
steps: Each impulse has area 2π/T, the same 50 265

d^{n}x(t)/dt^{n} ‖ (jω)^{n} X(jω).title: Differentiation (Fourier transform property)
d^{n}x(t)/dt^{n} ‖ (jω)^{n} X(jω).about: Each derivative multiplies the spectrum by jω, boosting high frequencies. It turns linear differential equations into algebra.
assumptions: x and its derivatives have transforms

example.problem: Find H(jω) for dy/dt + 2y = x(t) and evaluate it at ω = 2 rad/s.

y(t) = x(t) ∗ h(t) ‖ Y(jω) = X(jω) H(jω).title: Convolution property
y(t) = x(t) ∗ h(t) ‖ Y(jω) = X(jω) H(jω).about: Convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency. An LTI system's output spectrum is the input spectrum times the frequency response.

example.problem: x(t) = cos(2t) enters H(jω) = 1/(1 + jω). Find the output's amplitude.
steps: A sinusoid comes out at the same frequency scaled by |H(j2)|

y(t) = x(t) p(t) ‖ Y(jω) = (1/2π) X(jω).title: Multiplication (modulation) property
y(t) = x(t) p(t) ‖ Y(jω) = (1/2π) X(jω).about: Multiplying two signals convolves their spectra (with 1/2π). Multiplying by a cosine shifts the spectrum to ±ω_{o}: amplitude modulation.

example.problem: A message band-limited to 5 kHz multiplies a 100 kHz carrier. What band does the product occupy?
steps: P(jω) has impulses at ±ω_{c}; convolving shifts X to ±100 kHz at half height

x(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}} X(jω).title: Time shift (Fourier transform property)
x(t − t_{0}) ‖ e^{−jωt_{0}} X(jω).about: A delay leaves |X| unchanged and adds a phase −ωt_{0} that grows linearly with frequency.

example.problem: e^{−t}u(t) is delayed by 1 s. Find the transform at ω = 1 rad/s.
steps: |Y| = 0.707, same as before; only phase changed

e^{jω_{o}t} x(t) ‖ X(j(ω − ω_{o})).title: Frequency shift (Fourier transform property)
e^{jω_{o}t} x(t) ‖ X(j(ω − ω_{o})).about: Multiplying by a complex exponential slides the whole spectrum to the right by ω_{o}. Real modulation by cos does this in both directions.
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: x(t) = e^{−t}u(t) times e^{j10t}. Find the new spectrum at ω = 10 rad/s.
example.answer: Y(j10) = 1, the old peak moved to ω = 10

x(at) ‖ (1/|a|) X(jω/a).title: Time scaling (Fourier transform property)
x(at) ‖ (1/|a|) X(jω/a).about: Compressing a signal in time (|a| > 1) stretches its spectrum and lowers it. Short pulses need wide bandwidth.
assumptions: a real and nonzero; a negative also reverses time

example.problem: x(t) = e^{−t}u(t) is played twice as fast, x(2t). Find its transform at ω = 2 rad/s.

x(−t) ‖ X(−jω).title: Time reversal (Fourier transform property)
x(−t) ‖ X(−jω).about: Flipping time flips frequency. For a real signal X(−jω) = X^{*}(jω), so the magnitude stays and the phase changes sign.

example.problem: Find the transform of e^{3t}u(−t) at ω = 4 rad/s.

t x(t) ‖ j dX(jω)/dω.title: Multiplication by t (frequency differentiation)
t x(t) ‖ j dX(jω)/dω.about: Multiplying by t in time differentiates the spectrum. It generates pairs like t e^{−at}u(t).

example.problem: Derive the transform of t e^{−at}u(t).

∫_{−∞}^{t} x(τ) dτ ‖ X(jω)/(jω) + πX(0)δ.title: Integration (Fourier transform property)
∫_{−∞}^{t} x(τ) dτ ‖ X(jω)/(jω) + πX(0)δ.about: Integrating divides the spectrum by jω, attenuating high frequencies. The impulse accounts for the DC value the integral picks up when x has nonzero area.
assumptions: The impulse term vanishes when X(0) = ∫x dt = 0

example.problem: Find the transform of the step u(t) as the integral of δ(t).

X(jt) ‖ 2πx(−ω).title: Duality
X(jt) ‖ 2πx(−ω).about: If x(t) ↔ X(jω), using X's shape as a time signal gives 2π times x's shape reversed in frequency. Every pair gives you a second pair for free.
assumptions: Swap the roles of t and ω

example.problem: Use e^{−|t|} ↔ 2/(1 + ω^{2}) to find the transform of 2/(1 + t^{2}), and its value at ω = 1.

∫ |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ (1/2π) ∫ |X(jω)|^{2} d.title: Parseval's relation (CT Fourier transform)
∫ |x(t)|^{2} dt ‖ (1/2π) ∫ |X(jω)|^{2} d.about: Energy is the same whether summed in time or in frequency; |X(jω)|^{2}/2π is the energy density per rad/s.

example.problem: Find the energy of e^{−t}u(t) both ways.

Analysis ‖ X(e^{jω}) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n].title: Discrete-time Fourier transform (analysis)
Analysis ‖ X(e^{jω}) = Σ_{n=−∞}^{∞} x[n].about: Gives the spectrum of a sequence. It is periodic in ω with period 2π, and ω = π is the highest frequency a sequence can hold (half the sample rate).
assumptions: Converges if x is absolutely summable, Σ|x[n]| < ∞
Periodic and sinusoidal sequences need impulses
ω in rad/sample; physical frequency f = ωf_{s}/2π
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π
related: from the z-transform, if the unit circle is in the ROC

example.problem: Find X(e^{jω}) for x[n] = {1, 1} at n = 0, 1, and evaluate it at ω = π/2.

Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jω.title: Inverse discrete-time Fourier transform (synthesis)
Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jω.about: Rebuilds a sequence from one period of its spectrum. Because X is 2π-periodic, the integral runs over any interval of length 2π.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) is the DTFT of x[n]
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: An ideal DT low-pass has H = 1 for |ω| < π/4. Find h[0].

a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^{−jω}).title: Geometric sequence and its DTFT
a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^{−jω}).about: A one-sided geometric sequence, the impulse response of a first-order recursive filter y[n] = ay[n − 1] + x[n]. 0 < a < 1 gives a low-pass; −1 < a < 0 a high-pass.
assumptions: |a| < 1 so the sum converges; for |a| ≥ 1 there is no DTFT

example.problem: For h[n] = 0.5^{n}u[n], find |H| at ω = 0 and ω = π.
steps: A low-pass: gain 2 at DC, 0.667 at the highest frequency

(n + 1) a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^.title: Ramped geometric sequence and its DTFT
(n + 1) a^{n} u[n], |a| < 1 ‖ 1/(1 − ae^.about: The DT counterpart of t e^{−at}u(t): a double pole, the response of two identical first-order stages in cascade.

example.problem: Find X at ω = 0 for a = 0.5, and check against the sum.

δ[n] ‖ 1.title: Unit impulse and its DTFT
δ[n] ‖ 1.about: The unit sample has a flat spectrum. A filter's impulse response h[n] therefore has DTFT H(e^{jω}), its frequency response.

example.problem: Find the DTFT of 4δ[n] at ω = π/3.

δ[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}}.title: Delayed unit sample and its DTFT
δ[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}}.about: A delay of n_{o} samples has unit gain and a linear phase −ωn_{o}.

example.problem: Find the DTFT of δ[n − 2] at ω = π/4.

u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − e^{−jω}) + πδ(ω).title: Unit step sequence and its DTFT
u[n] ‖ 1/(1 − e^{−jω}) + πδ(ω).about: The step is a running sum of δ[n], so its DTFT is 1/(1 − e^{−jω}) plus an impulse for its DC value 1/2.
assumptions: Generalised transform: u[n] is not absolutely summable
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
related: Σ_{k≤n} x[k] ↔ X/(1 − e^{−jω}) + πX(e^{j0}) Σ δ(ω − 2πk)

example.problem: Find U(e^{jω}) at ω = π.

e^{jω_{o}n} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).title: DT complex exponential and its DTFT
e^{jω_{o}n} ‖ 2πδ(ω − ω_{o}).about: One spectral line at ω_{o}, repeated every 2π. Frequencies ω_{o} and ω_{o} + 2π give the same sequence.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

steps: They are the same sequence; check at n = 1: e^{j9π/4} = 0.7071 + 0.7071j

cos(ω_{o}n) ‖ πδ(ω − ω_{o}) + πδ(ω + ω_{.about: Two lines of area π at ±ω_{o} in each period. A DT cosine is periodic only if ω_{o}/2π is rational.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
0 ≤ ω_{o} ≤ π for a unique frequency
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: A 1 kHz tone is sampled at 8 kHz. Where are its lines?

sin(ω_{o}n) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.title: DT sine and its DTFT
sin(ω_{o}n) ‖ (π/j)[δ(ω − ω_{o}) − δ(ω +.about: Two lines at ±ω_{o} with imaginary areas −jπ and +jπ in each period.
assumptions: X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential

example.problem: Find the area of the line at +ω_{o} for 3 sin(0.2πn).

sin(Wn)/(πn), 0 < W < π ‖ 1 for |ω| < W,.about: The impulse response of an ideal DT low-pass filter with cutoff W; truncated and windowed, it is the start of FIR filter design.
assumptions: At n = 0 the value is W/π
X(e^{jω}) repeats every 2π; the pair shows one period

example.problem: Find h[0] and h[1] for an ideal low-pass with W = π/2.

1 for |n| ≤ N_{1}, 0 else ‖ sin(ω(N_{1}.about: A pulse of 2N_{1} + 1 ones has a periodic sinc (Dirichlet kernel) spectrum, equal to 2N_{1} + 1 at ω = 0 with zeros at multiples of 2π/(2N_{1} + 1).
vars: half-width of the pulse, in samples

example.problem: For N_{1} = 2 (five ones), find X at ω = π/2.

x[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}} X(e^{jω}).title: Time shift (DTFT property)
x[n − n_{o}] ‖ e^{−jωn_{o}} X(e^{jω}).about: Delaying by n_{o} samples adds a linear phase −ωn_{o} and leaves |X| alone.
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: x[n] = 0.5^{n}u[n] is delayed by 1. Find its DTFT at ω = π/2.

y[n] = x[n] ∗ h[n] ‖ Y(e^{jω}) = X(e^{jω.title: Convolution property (DTFT)
y[n] = x[n] ∗ h[n] ‖ Y(e^{jω}) = X(e^{jω.about: A DT LTI system multiplies the input spectrum by its frequency response H(e^{jω}).

example.problem: A two-point average h = {0.5, 0.5} filters cos(πn/2). Find the output amplitude.

e^{jω_{o}n} x[n] ‖ X(e^{j(ω − ω_{o})}).title: Frequency shift (DTFT property)
e^{jω_{o}n} x[n] ‖ X(e^{j(ω − ω_{o})}).about: Multiplying by e^{jω_{o}n} slides the spectrum by ω_{o}. With ω_{o} = π, (−1)^{n}x[n] turns a low-pass into a high-pass.
vars: frequency of the sinusoid or exponential
DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: h[n] = 0.5^{n}u[n] is low-pass. Find the gain at ω = π of (−1)^{n}h[n].
steps: G(e^{jω}) = H(e^{j(ω − π)}); at ω = π it is H(e^{j0})

x[−n] ‖ X(e^{−jω}).title: Time reversal (DTFT property)
x[−n] ‖ X(e^{−jω}).about: Reversing a sequence reverses its spectrum; for real x it conjugates it.
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the DTFT of 0.5^{−n}u[−n] at ω = π/2.

n x[n] ‖ j dX(e^{jω})/dω.title: Multiplication by n (DTFT property)
n x[n] ‖ j dX(e^{jω})/dω.about: Multiplying a sequence by n differentiates its spectrum.
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the DTFT of n a^{n}u[n].

x[n] − x[n − 1] ‖ (1 − e^{−jω}) X(e^{jω}.title: First difference (DTFT property)
x[n] − x[n − 1] ‖ (1 − e^{−jω}) X(e^{jω}.about: The DT stand-in for a derivative: a high-pass that blocks DC and doubles the highest frequency.
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the first difference's gain at ω = 0, π/2 and π.

x[n] y[n] ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jθ}) Y(e^.title: Multiplication (DTFT property)
x[n] y[n] ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} X(e^{jθ}) Y(e^.about: Multiplying two sequences convolves their spectra periodically over one 2π period. Windowing a sequence smears its spectrum this way.

example.problem: x[n] is multiplied by cos(πn/2). Where does a spectral line of x at ω = 0.1 go?
steps: cos(πn/2) has lines at ±π/2 with area π; the (1/2π) gives half height

Σ_{n} |x[n]|^{2} ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} |X(e^{j.title: Parseval's relation (DTFT)
Σ_{n} |x[n]|^{2} ‖ (1/2π) ∫_{2π} |X(e^{j.about: A sequence's energy equals the spectrum's energy averaged over one period.
vars: DTFT of x[n], periodic in ω with period 2π

example.problem: Find the energy of 0.5^{n}u[n].

Analysis ‖ X[k] = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} x[n] e^{.about: Samples one period of the DTFT of an N-point sequence at the N frequencies ω_{k} = 2πk/N. The FFT computes it fast.
assumptions: x[n] has N points (pad with zeros for a finer frequency grid)
X[k] is periodic in k with period N
Bin k is the frequency kf_{s}/N

Synthesis ‖ x[n] = (1/N) Σ_{k=0}^{N−1} X.about: Rebuilds the N samples from the N DFT coefficients. The 1/N goes here in the usual convention.
assumptions: Treats x as one period of an N-periodic sequence

example.problem: A 4-point DFT is X = {10, −2 + 2j, −2, −2 − 2j}. Find x[0].
